memo:
I have decided that all 125 affected people will be retrained and moved into plant roles, keeping their current pay. None will be eliminated, and none will take the 40% pay cut that the plant-pay path would impose on business and financial operations staff.

The work itself is saved on every path, so the choice is about the people. Eliminating roles would save the most in year one but would end 125 livelihoods and withdraw skilled workers from the communities where the plants operate. Severance of about $8,902 a person does not replace that.

The cost of this path over the next four quarters is about $9.7 million: $7.6 million for retraining and training-period pay (125 at $60,600 each, once) and $2.1 million for the pay gap. That is roughly 1.3% of last year's net income of $162.4 million, and it is covered by the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. Office and administrative staff account for only about $0.06 million of the pay gap, because their current pay is close to the plant rate. Most of the cost sits with business and financial operations staff.

Plant roles are the same roles the Company hires 500 people a year to fill from outside. Filling 125 of them internally reduces external hiring, keeps experienced staff, and avoids the disruption of layoffs. The retraining cost is recovered in about two years.

Risks: the pay gap is ongoing, not one-time, and it should be reviewed when the four quarters close. If cash or earnings come under pressure, the plant-pay path for some business and financial staff is the fallback, at a cost to those employees. I recommend the board monitor retention and productivity in the plants through the year, and I will report on whether the 125 moves are holding.

I have chosen to move all 125 affected people into plant roles at their current pay. No one loses a job or takes a pay cut, and the Company still captures the full $11.4 million a year saving from work that is no longer needed.

The cost is $7.6 million one-time for retraining: $15,000 a person for instruction, plus $5.7 million of pay and benefits during six months of training. There is also a $2.1 million a year pay difference, paid for as long as people hold plant roles. That difference is about 1.3% of the $162.4 million net income and is fully covered by the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level.

Elimination would have cost only $1.1 million in severance, but it would put 125 people out of work and forgo filling plant roles that the Company would otherwise hire for from outside. Moving at plant pay would cut pay by 39.8% for business and financial operations staff on average, which would likely drive out the experienced people we most need to keep.

Customers and suppliers are unaffected by this choice. The plants gain people who already know the Company's products, and the moves cover 125 of the roughly 500 external hires a year, which supports the retraining payback. Environmental spending is unchanged.

Risks: the pay gap between transferred staff and plant colleagues doing similar work could cause friction. I will ask HR to manage this openly and to move people to plant pay through attrition over time, which reduces the ongoing cost. I recommend the board review the arrangement at the four-quarter mark against retention, productivity and the realised cost.

I am placing all 125 affected people on the retrain-and-move path that keeps current pay. The work is eliminated on every path, so the choice concerns who bears the cost of the change.

Eliminating roles is cheapest in cash terms ($1.1 million of severance), but it puts 125 people out of work, with a median of about four years' service, and offers each roughly $8,900. That places the heaviest cost on employees and on the communities where they live, and it discards experience the plants need, since they hire about 500 people a year from outside.

Moving at the plant role's pay costs less once (about $7.6 million including training pay). However, it would cut business and financial operations staff's pay by about 40%, asking the people least able to absorb it to carry most of the cost of change.

Keeping current pay costs about $9.6 million in the first year, including retraining and training pay, plus a pay difference of about $2.1 million a year thereafter. This is affordable from the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum, and it is offset by the $11.4 million of work cost removed on every path. The first-year gap to the cheaper path is about $2 million, roughly 1.2% of net income. Shareholders bear a modest, visible cost. Employees avoid layoffs and pay cuts, customers keep continuity of service, suppliers keep steady orders, and communities avoid job losses. The plants also fill roles they would otherwise hire for externally.

I will track the ongoing pay difference against hiring savings each quarter and revisit the mix if the cost grows beyond what the business can support.

I have decided that no one in the 125 affected roles will be made redundant. All 125 will be retrained and moved into plant roles, which the plants need anyway: they hire about 500 people a year from outside, and these employees can fill those openings.

I split the group 65 at plant pay and 60 keeping current pay, with the split applied in the same proportion to office and administrative support and to business and financial operations. Plant pay is the sustainable base. It costs no recurring premium, and the roles are ones the Company must fill regardless. Office staff take only a 1.5% reduction, but business and financial staff face a 39.8% cut, which is severe and risks losing the people we are retraining. Keeping current pay for 60 people protects that group from the steepest cuts. It costs about $1.0 million a year in premiums, roughly 0.6% of net income. Shareholders bear that cost, which I accept as a reasonable trade for employees and for retention.

The one-time retraining cost is about $7.6 million, covering $15,000 per person for instruction and $45,600 per person for pay during six months of training. I recognise that eliminating roles would cost far less in year one, about $1.1 million in severance, and that the retraining cost is not recovered within four quarters. But severance would remove 125 jobs from our communities while the plants are hiring externally. Retraining pays back within about two years against outside hiring, and it keeps skills and experience inside the Company.

Cash above the minimum operating level covers these costs. Customers, suppliers and the environment are not directly affected. I will monitor retention in the two functions and the cost of the premium through the year, and I will report to the board at the next quarter.

I have assigned all 125 affected people to the path that moves them into plant roles at their current pay (move_keep_pay). The work of their roles is removed on every path, so the choice concerns the people, not the cost of the work.

Eliminating roles would cost only about $8,900 a person in severance, but it ends the pay of 125 people who know our machines and customers, and the plants would then hire from outside for the same positions. Moving at plant pay would cut business and financial operations staff by about 40% ($36,569 a year each) and office staff by 1.5%. I will not impose that on 55 people when the Company can afford to keep their pay.

Keep-pay costs about $77,200 per person in the year: $15,000 retraining, $45,600 of training pay and benefits, and about $16,600 of pay difference. For 125 people that is about $9.6 million, roughly 22% of the $44.1 million cash above the minimum, leaving about $34.5 million. Compared with severance, this lowers year-one profit by about $8.5 million, around 5% of net income. I accept that as the price of keeping jobs and pay. The pay difference of $2.1 million a year continues while people hold plant roles, so I will ask the board to review it at year end against plant-role pay and productivity.

The moves fill roles the plants would otherwise hire for from outside, so the Company keeps experienced staff, the communities keep their jobs, and suppliers and customers keep a stable workforce. Dividends and repurchases are unaffected by this decision.

I have placed all 125 affected people on the retrain-and-keep-current-pay path, with no eliminations and no moves at plant-role pay.

Eliminating roles is the cheapest option in cash, about $8,900 severance per person, but it removes 125 jobs from employees and the communities around our plants. The work is going away, but these people are not surplus to our plant needs: we hire about 500 people a year into the same production, maintenance and warehouse roles. Moving them into those roles fills positions we would otherwise hire for.

Moving at plant-role pay would cut business and financial operations staff by 39.8% ($36,569 a year). That is a severe cut to 55 people, and the likely result is attrition, which would waste the $7.6 million we would spend on retraining and training pay. Because the numbers must apply in the same proportion to both functions, I cannot protect the business staff while moving the office staff at plant pay, and I do not think the plant-pay path is acceptable for them.

Keeping current pay costs about $16,560 a person a year, or $2.1 million a year for the group. Over the next four quarters, total cash cost is about $9.7 million: $1.9 million of retraining, $5.7 million of pay during training, and $2.1 million of pay difference. That is covered by the $44.1 million of cash above our minimum operating level, and about 1.3% of this year's net income. The $11.4 million annual saving from the removed work is achieved on this path too.

Shareholders bear a modest recurring cost. In return, employees keep their income, the Company keeps trained people for roles it needs to fill, and customers and communities keep the same skills and continuity. I will review the pay difference when these roles are next priced.

I have placed all 125 affected people on the path that retrains them into plant roles and keeps their current pay. The work of these 125 roles is eliminated on every path, so this decision concerns the people, not the savings.

Cost: one-time retraining of $1.9 million plus $5.7 million of pay and benefits during training, $7.6 million in all, fundable from the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. Most of it falls on the 55 business and financial operations staff, whose plant-role pay would be 40% below their current pay.

Why this path: it keeps every affected person's income intact, which the plant-pay path would not for business and financial operations staff. Eliminating the roles would save about $1.1 million in severance, but it would leave 125 people out of work while the plants hire about 500 people from outside. That harms employees and the communities where they live. Retraining fills plant roles that would otherwise be filled by outside hiring, giving production, maintenance and warehouse work trained people and keeping service and parts supply steady for customers.

Risks: the pay difference is a commitment for as long as people hold plant roles. I ask the board to review it each year against plant hiring needs, and to track whether retrained staff stay and perform. Shareholders bear a real cost of about $2.1 million a year. I judge that acceptable against the outcome for employees, customers and communities over the coming four quarters.

The board should review whether transitional support is warranted for the business and financial operations group, since the numbers apply in the same proportion to both functions and I cannot target that support within this decision.

I recommend retraining all 125 affected people into plant roles and eliminating none. But the plants hire about 500 people a year from outside into roles these employees can fill after retraining. Retraining therefore turns a job loss into a substitution for an outside hire, which keeps 125 households employed and protects the communities around the plants. I am moving all 125 affected people into plant roles on their current pay, with retraining. The cost is real.
